Public Service-Salary Deduction

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
I am sure every member of the
house, with the exception of those who occupy the treasury benches, would much rather that we had before us for consideration some measure to provide for the relief of the unemployed than to provide a reduction in the salaries of those who are now employed; but inasmuch as the government has not seen fit so far to bring in such a measure, and inasmuch as this resolution is now before us, I have no alternative but to discuss it.
Last Friday evening when the house adjourned I was discussing the resolution and I pointed out at that time that the government was setting an example to private employers throughout the country to reduce still further salaries and wages paid by them. I said that hon. gentlemen opposite were setting this example by reducing the salaries and wages of government employees, and doing so in an arbitrary manner without any negotiations with those affected. The government, I pointed out, had already repudiated the principle of collective bargaining by refusing to negotiate on the question of reducing salaries and wages. I had quoted from order in council P.C. 1743 of July 11, 1918, and order in council P.C. 880 of May 1, 1919, in which the government had announced the principle of collective bargaining. Further, I had pointed out that the parliament of Canada had adopted the principle of collective bargaining and had endorsed and recommended the principle of establishing a civil service council to take care of just such matters as we have before us at the present time.
I was in the midst of my remarks at eleven o'clock on Friday night when the house adjourned, and I was reading into the record the provisions contained in order in council P.C. 970 of May 7, 1930. I do not think it is necessary to read any further, because the provisions of that order in council are well known. The order in council was the outcome of the assurance of the Liberal party to the civil service of this country that such a civil service council would be established, and it was as well the result of the deliberations of parliament. I need only tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in addition to what I have already read into the record, the order in council provides for the composition of the council, and how it should be called; and the last paragraph makes provision for travelling expenses incurred by the representatives of the civil service coming from different parts of the country. The eleventh or last paragraph reads:
It is recommended that travelling expenses incidental to attending the committee's meetings incurred by those attending from points other than Ottawa should be defrayed by the government. It is further recommended that civil service organizations' representatives attending the meetings of the committee shall be accorded special leave of absence, with pay, for the purpose by their respective departments.
Now that provision has been entirely ignored by the present government. Indeed,
I read in the newspapers that the government had indicated that they were not favourable to such a measure. I know that excuses can be made by the present government; they can say that they were not in sympathy with a measure of this kind. But it has been my experience that anyone who is not favourable to any principle can easily find an excuse for its repudiation. So that this reduction in salaries and wages now contemplated is being made without proper representations, or proper hearing or negotiations on the part of the parties affected.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in his speech a few days ago read a letter from a lady in the civil service signifying her satisfaction with the cut in her salary. My experience has always been-and I have had a long experience along this line-that in every such movement, whether it be increases or decreases in wages, you will find the exceptional person, the one who is ever ready to signify to the boss that he or she is not like the others but is perfectly satisfied with the position they hold. But why does not the Prime Minister read all the correspondence he has received? Why does he not read all the letters he has had for and against the reduction in salaries, and give the names of those who have forwarded them to him? Then the house would be in a better position to judge whether or not the civil servants are satisfied.
The Conservative party when in opposition pretended to have great sympathy with low-paid civil servants. I can see their tears now, rolling down their cheeks, when they were sitting on this side of the house, over the poor and lowly civil servants. It would not be fair for me to say that at that time they were bidding for power; that would be unparliamentary. I would suggest that they were not playing politics at all. But we have examples. We find that on May 21, 1928, at page 3241 of Hansard for that year, Mr. Manion had this to say with respect to the lowly paid civil servants:
One thousand and eighty dollars is $90 a month, and $90 a month is not sufficient for these men to live decently on and support their families.
.	COMMONS
Public Service-Salary Deduction
The Mr. Manion of that time is the Hon. Mr. Manion now, a member of this cabinet who now appears on the floor of this house supporting a further reduction of civil servants' salaries.
Then, we have the utterances of the gentleman who is now Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett): I find that in Hansard of March 21, 1930, at page 858, Mr. Bennett is quoted as follows:
I am sure the Minister of Justice will say that no man can live and maintain a family on $65 a month. That is the reason I have always favoured a minimum salary of $100 a month for the civil service.
The gentleman who uttered those words is to-day Prime Minister of Canada. He has it in his power to give the lower paid civil servants $100 a month, but instead of doing that we find he is cutting their present wage by ten per cent. This statement of the Prime Minister, the then leader of the opposition, was broadcast not. only throughout Ottawa but throughout the country. It was an example of his instructions given to Conservative speakers during the last election, as shown by the speakers' hand book. This statement I have quoted was set out in large capital letters, and of course the civil servants of Canada were not supposed to read them.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, your intervention saved me a great deal of trouble. I thought I was going to have to call the member to order myself.
The words I have quoted were those of the Prime Minister addressed to the civil ser-
vants in 1930. Let us compare his words on that occasion with his present views when Prime Minister of Canada. We find that Hansard of February 8, 1932, page 59 contains the following statement:
But looking about us, realizing our obligations, and desiring that the people of this country should understand fully that the government is anxious to lead the way with respect to matters of economy, we have concluded that we will ask this parliament to pass a statute to reduce by ten per cent the indemnities alike of the Senate and of the Commons, and of the compensation paid to ministers and to every branch of the public service. That must be effected.
I am wondering where his sympathy for civil servants has gone, in view of the fact that in the year 1930 he declared that $100 was a minimum salary.
The government of Canada surely is leading the way towards salary and wage reductions, and those reductions quite evidently are having their effect throughout the country because we see, hear and read of wages being reduced in practically every industry. It is quite evident that the salary cut in certain circles has been well planned and well understood. The wages of railroad men including employees of the government's own railroad, have been reduced, and we have heard no protests from any members of the cabinet. Instead of protests, as a matter of fact it would seem that both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways have approved of the action taken by the government railways. It is quite evident the government is satisfied.
I needed no evidence to assure me however, because even before the cut took place I knew the government would approve of it.
Let us compare the attitude of the government with that of the mayor of the city of Toronto. In that city the question of salary cuts was before the city council and in that connection the mayor is reported in the Globe newspaper of February 27, 1932, as follows:
"If we give leadership, are we not asking private enterprise to follow suit? The city will simply be giving the cloak of respectability to a wage-cut on the part of private enterprise, said the mayor. "I have a letter from a large employer of labour who is opposing the wage reduction."
I want to take off my hat to the mayor of the city of Toronto. The working men of Canada know now who is setting the example and leading the pace. In their minds and in mine there is no one to blame but the present government of Canada. Not only are they leading the way in the reduction of wages and salaries but also in the discharge of em-

Let us for example consider the recent dismissals, releases or whatever you wish to call them in the Department of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland). I am informed that 75 flying officers have been released. Where will those men find employment to-day? They will find themselves lined up with the boys we saw at the gate to-day looking for work. I am advised that 42 of those men served overseas in the great war, and that 38 of them are married with dependent children. At one time in their lives they offered to sacrifice their all for the defence of the British Empire, and I can well recall some of our politicians going around the country telling those boys that they were going to make Canada a place fit for heroes to live in. Now, when they are performing services of a useful character, their services are no longer required. Undoubtedly they could perform useful work; for instance, they could be sent into the Patricia district to see whether or not those Indians are dying, and whether their children are going blind as was reported in the press. It is not sufficient for this government to say that they have heard from some Hudson's Bay factor that the report is incorrect. Some of those flying officers ought to be used to ascertain whether or not there is need for assistance in that outlying country. But the government has discharged those flying officers and thrown them on the mercy of the world, not caring what will become of them. And if the British Empire needed them to-morrow they would be the first men expected to get into harness and defend it.

speechtext:
I was amused the other day, Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister in introducing this motion read a letter to the house purporting to come from some lady in 'the civil service to the effect that she was glad to take the proposed reduction. I do not know whether it is because I am a married man, but I have received no communications from any ladies in the civil service; I have received communications from many men and representatives of civil servants protesting against the salary cut. The other day I met a civil servant who said to me: I am getting $100 a month; out of this I have to pay 5 per cent towards my pension fund, and the proposed 10 per cent reduction will leave me only $85 a month to maintain my wife and six Children. I do not see how any married man in the city of Ottawa can expect to do that on $85 a month. True, the Prime Minister has stated that in the case of the lower salaries the 5 per cent superannuation will be paid by the government, but still the salary cut leaves such men in a difficult position.
Last session during the debate on the budget, I made the statement that so far as I could see the only people the budget favoured were those of the wealthy class. Looking through the current estimates I find that the only people getting any benefit are those who are lending money to the government. As compared with the interest paid last year to the money lenders, this year the amount will be increased by something like $13,000,000. The Minister of Finance may retort: Well, many small bondholders are getting this interest; many widows and others who have invested $1,000, $2,000 or $3,000 in these bonds are getting a part of the interest. Probably that is so. But I venture to say 'that within six months or a year, if conditions continue as they are to-day, and if the government does not change its policy in order to improve conditions-and they will never improve until the government does Change its policy-most of these bonds that to-day are in the hands of widows and other small investors will be in the hands of the big investors; they will have full control just as they secured control of the war bonds shortly after 'they were issued, especially the tax-exempt bonds. I submit that when the national service loan was floated it could have been floated easily at 4 per cent instead of at 5|- per cent, and 'thus the government could have saved the country a lot of money in interest payments.

The other day the Prime Minister stated that judges and army and navy officers were exempt from this proposed salary cut. How can you compare the position of a man who has to maintain a wife and six children on $85 a month with the position of a judge getting $9,000 a year and making no contribution to the pension which he gets on a very liberal scale when he retires? As a reason for this exemption it was stated that the judges' salaries are statutory. Well, this parliament is supreme, all-powerful; as it can make, so it can unmake; it can amend or repeal any statute. Last session we amended the Judges Act so that the Chief Justice of Manitoba by his acceptance of the chairmanship of the Board of Railway Commissioners should in no way prejudice his pension rights.
I am against this reduction unless it is graded, and unless it takes in the high-salaried officers of the army and navy, and the judges. I think the government will be ill-advised if they do not follow that course; I am sure it would be to their benefit, politically and otherwise, if they included everyone in this measure.
We have heard a great deal to the effect that conditions in Canada are better than in the United States, but the civil service of the United States is in a better condition than is the civil service of Canada. President Hoover said he would veto any measure proposing a reduction in the salaries of the civil service, but that he would approve of statutory increases being withheld. At the frontier ports between Canada and the United States, their men start at a salary of $2,000 a year, while ours start at a salary of $1,200. Their lowest paid clerk receives $1,700 a year. I know of one man who has been with the customs department for twenty-six years; he is a sub-collector, and he receives $2,340. Right next to him the United States subcollector receives $2,900. So I do not think we should brag any more about Canada being in a better condition than the United States; we are paying smaller salaries and now we are asking these officials to take a cut of ten per cent.
Personally, if the Prime Minister had come to me and said, "We need $400 of your indemnity to help carry the country through,"
I do not think I would have refused to give that amount, but I do not think it fair that I should be asked to give $400 of my indemnity while people receiving high salaries are taking no reduction at all. They do not have to carry on elections; they have no expense of that kind; they are not at the beck and call of every charitable and begging organiza-

tion in the country. I am not criticising those organizations at all; no doubt they do a good work, but surely there is as much justification for taking SI,000 from the salary of one of these men as there is for taking $400 from my indemnity. Unless the judges and the highly paid officers of the army and navy are included in this reduction and unless the reduction is graded so that the people receiving small salaries will be relieved and will have a chance to look after their families properly, I intend to vote against this resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few observations I have to make I do not propose to attack the evident intention of the government to exercise principles of economy; rather I intend to discuss very briefly the practical application of the resolution to the members of the civil service receiving small salaries.
Naturally a proposal to reduce the salaries paid those in the employ of the government always will produce a clash of opinion. It is to be expected that those directly affected will object to the reduction, and in addition we have those, not directly affected, who believe that it is not a sound principle to make any reduction whatever. In fact, not only in this particular connection but in other relationships we have two schools of thought, the one contending that wages should not be cut at all and that we should spend more, while the other says we should spend less. I think those who argue that if wages are cut, purchasing power will be diminished, production will be lessened and unemployment increased are making a fairly good argument, though possibly the question is debatable. We have had the question discussed from many points of view in connection with unemployment, and I must say that I have sometimes envied some hon. members of this house who have very cheerfully and very profoundly given their opinions and their reasons for those opinions on such matters as the cause of the depreciation of our currency, the effect of the adverse balance of trade, the cause of unemployment, and all that sort of thing. For my part I have felt, and feel now, considerable reluctance to rush in where angels might very well fear to tread. I prefer to consider this resolution from one point of view alone, and that is this: Whether it will be possible under the resolution and the bill which will be based upon it for some of those affected to maintain a decent scale of living, and whether it will be possible for them to 41761-48
have what they are entitled to, a reasonably comfortable subsistence for themselves and their families.
I think, Mr. Speaker, most of the people of this country will now admit that both individually and as a country we have lived pretty high and pretty expensively until the last two years. We have created debts which ten or twenty years ago we would have thought it absolutely impossible for this government to carry. I think I am right when I say that the federal debt, added to the provincial and municipal debts, totals over five billion dollars, on which evidently the interest must be in the neighbourhood of a quarter of a billion dollars a year. To my mind that is a very serious situation. It may be that sometime I will be converted to the theory that the way back to prosperity is to spend more; I hope my mind is always open to conviction, but I am still old fashioned enough to believe in the principles of thrift and the policy of spending a little less than we earn or than we receive, and that applies to governments as much as it does to individuals. However, that is always predicated on the fact to which I referred a moment ago, that men must earn enough to make saving possible. There is an irreducible minimum below which no Canadian, whether he is in the service of the government or in the service of a private concern, should be asked to live.
I am entirely sincere, and I have no axe to grind-I think my hon. friends opposite as well as my hon. friends on this side will believe me-when I say that I have every sympathy with the government in its efforts to balance the budget. We are told, I think on pretty good authority, that this year the deficit will be very heavy, between $75,000,000 and $100,000,000, without taking into account the heavy loss on the national railways, and probably those deficits will continue. I am not a pessimist when I make that statement; it is very likely that we will find it very difficult to make both ends meet for some time to come. We cannot indefinitely take care of deficits by increasing the debt or increasing the taxes, or both; that would mean national disaster in the end. Sometimes I am tempted -and I say this also with reluctance-to say that if it could be done in a practical way it might be a good thing for all concerned if we made a capital levy to wipe out this incubus of debt, at once or over a short period of years. I do not offer this as a serious suggestion at this time, but perhaps some day it might be worthy of consideration. Perhaps we might introduce the practice which pre-

vailed in days of old, in Palestine I think, where they had a year of jubilee every fifty years when all debts were wiped off. That might be not a bad principle to follow.
In order to balance a budget, the government has two methods at its command. One is to increase revenues, and I suppose in due course when the budget comes down we shall be able to note the measures to be taken to increase revenues by means of increased taxation. The other method is to decrease expenditure. The government is adopting to some extent this latter method in connection with the estimates which involve, as we all know, a decrease in the salaries of government employees. If I am any judge of public opinion I am inclined to believe that the country generally favours anything in the way of measures of economy. I am inclined also to believe that public opinion will support the government in making a reasonable reduction in the salaries of the higher salaried officials serving the country. The question is just where these reductions should end. I agree with the bon. member who has just spoken; I, too, have every sympathy with the man on a small salary whether he is serving the people of 'Canada or a private employer. To reduce the salary of a man who has *to support a family on $60, $70, $75, $100 or even $125 per month does not seem to me to be consistent with the principle which I have laid down, that a Canadian is entitled to a respectable and reasonably comfortable living *for himself and his family. This is where I take exception to the resolution.
There are those who have not very much sympathy with government employees. Some believe that there are too many of them, and in this I am inclined to agree but I think the efficient employee has not been too well paid in the past. It may be that a man living out in the country may think that a salary of $100 per month is large pay and that a man receiving such a salary could well afford to take a cut, but I think those who live in the city would say otherwise. Some reduction has taken place in the cost of living but I am afraid that a large proportion of that reduction has not reached the man who has a large family to support, at least it has not reached him to subh an extent that he finds relief in the problem of making a living for himself and his family. There are those who believe that government employees are already well protected by reason of the fact toat 'they are sure of their employment, but that is not true to-day because many government employees have been discharged from the service for reasons of economy. I am not a special 
advocate for those employed by the government, but I think I should point out that men have been attracted to the government service because of the sense of security therein even though -the pay was small. These men received a small remuneration as compared with those in private employment only a few years ago; while they were sure of their jobs they had no opportunities to make a little extra money by means of investments or even speculation. If, during the period of prosperity these men had to bear a disability from which others did not suffer, it does not seem to me to be quite fair to take from them the little advantage which they had when the period of prosperity comes to an end.
The government is also cutting off the statutory increases. Some may say that a man cannot lose what he never had, but I think it is true that these employees relied upon their receiving the increase which the statute granted them from year to year. These employees made certain commitments-a man might purchase a small home or he might take out a policy of life insurance, and so on -obligations from which they cannot escape, and with this additional cut they will find things to be very embarrassing and difficult.
I think the government as well as the hon. members of this house desire to follow the wishes of the Canadian people generally in connection with this matter. There has been some suggestion made that we on this side are playing politics, but it happens that I have not very many civil servants in my constituency, and I can hardly be accused of playing politics in this matter. I have received representations from the letter carriers and the civil servants generally; I have had them from the Trades and Labour Council of my city, from the business men's association, from the ratepayers associations and from the Canadian Legion, and these representations have all been along the line of my own thought, that the government should not make a cut in the salaries of employees who are now receiving a remuneration just sufficient to keep body and soul together. I make the suggestion to the government in all seriousness, that they again consider this matter, if they have not already done so, and frame their bill in such a way that those receiving up to $100, or perhaps $125 per month be not subjected to any reduction.

Mr. Speaker, the question before the house has already been debated at length, however I wish to explain briefly the vote which I shall probably be called upon to register.

The government asks us to adopt a resolution the effect of which is to cut down the salaries of civil servants by ten per cent. It is true that the government has to meet serious financial difficulties of which it is solely responsible. There are two ways of levying revenues: First by increasing taxation and helping commercial enterprises; secondly, by decreasing the expenditure.
The government through its high tariff policy, has not only cut down its revenues but has almost exhausted its resources. The revenues are, to-day, much less. If for the last two years a reasonable policy, one identical to that of the Liberal party in 1930, had been resorted to, foreign trade would have maintained itself, imports and exports would have continued, and the government would have had sufficient revenues.
The government contends that it practises economy, but such is not the case. No matter where we turn, we discover that instead of economizing, the government displays extravagance in its administration. What is the situation? To quote only what took place in my constituency, the government appointed, since the last election, a large number of commissioners to hold inquiries, whose main work, in fact their only occupation, was to travel through the rural districts in order to ascertain who were the civil servants that sided with the opposition. There is not a post office to be found where the incumbent was suspected to be friendly to the Liberal party. These commissioners are still travelling through the country holding expensive inquiries. This government, sir, has also money to throw away to carry on inquiries as insignificant as the one relating to the travelling expenses of a certain Mr. Herridge. Although we must show respect to the Prime Minister of a country, however, one must not be led away to the extent of thinking that the honeymoon trip of Mr. Herridge or the Prime Minister's sister has such importance that we should have to spend enormous sums to inquire into events that are of no interest to the ratepayers of this country. If the government wishes to be extravagant in matters of this kind, I think it should not do so at the expense of our civil servants. In my opinion, the civil servants are not over paid, and furthermore, with the exception of two or three, I contend that they are not sufficiently remunerated.
Considering that the government should adopt other methods to increase its revenues, I shall be pleased to vote against this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I feel I cannot let this resolution pass without stating my position and I do so to-day more particularly because I was in 1929 as Postmaster General of Canada, the subject of one of the greatest onslaughts ever made upon a minister of the crown by the opposition of the day in an attempt to convince me that the lower salaried officials should have their salaries increased. At that time we saw the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), then in opposition, the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), then in opposition, the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), then in opposition, as well as the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), then leading the opposition, appeal to the then government to increase the salaries of those who were employed at a salary of under 81,000 a year. For the information of the house and particularly of those members now here who did not occupy seats in this chamber at that time, I wish to call attention to some of the statements made on that occasion by the hon. gentlemen whom I have just mentioned. As reported on page 1874 of Hansard of 1929, I find the present Minister of Justice making this statement:
When it comes to the higher grade salaries they are not niggardly, they are fairly generous; when it comes to a question of increasing the salaries of gentlemen of technical or professional knowledge, they take other means of getting round the Civil Service Act. ... I believe that the lower grades of the civil service in Canada have been very badly treated by this government.
How are they being treated now, may I ask?
They have sent those unfortunate people from pillar to post.
Where are they being sent now? There is not even a post for them upon which to rest their shoulders. They cannot find a pillar from which they may expect some solace. The same hon. gentleman continues on page 2180:
I submit that the present salaries paid the lower grade officials in the postal service is a disgrace to Canada and to the public service, and should not be tolerated in this great country.
What has the hon. gentleman to say now when he is reducing those disgraceful salaries, as he called them at that time, to an even more disgraceful amount than they were in 1929? He continues:
I would not suggest giving them a niggardly $60 increase as recommended by the Postmaster General.

May I to-day be permitted to appeal to the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and ask him to appeal to the new Minister of Finance, to attempt to soften his heart and not to make the ten per cent reduction against the men who were underpaid at that time. Oh, the answer will come back that living is cheaper to-day than it was in 1929 and 1930. The figures given the other day by the Prime Minister or some other minister showed a reduction of fourteen per cent in the cost of living, and the idea was that this reduction of ton per cent in salaries would be within the mark. Let me point out that the present Minister of Justice, speaking on one of the occasions in 1929 to which I have referred, stated that the cost of living at that time

was $1,122.60 a year, and that for the mere necessaries of life for a family of five. That is a reduction of fourteen per cent, which leaves $965. Take the minimum salary paid officials in the Post Office Department, letter carriers and so forth. If you take ten per cent off what does it leave? It leaves them $972, merely five or six dollars above what the fourteen per cent reduction in the cost of living leaves them for the bare necessaries of life. And these are the gentlemen now occupying the government benches, whose tears flowed quite freely in 1929 on behalf of these poor, underpaid officials. There they sit to-day no doubt prepared to vote unanimously, as they have adopted unanimously in council, the reduction of ten per cent against these men. In the name of conscience, what reason can they give for it to-day? Let me quote the Minister of Trade and Commerce of to-day (Mr. Stevens) to show what his attitude was when he was in opposition in 1929. The hon. gentleman after appealing to the ministers of the government to be generous, said:
We have urged the government to take action. We have assured the government of our support, but we have failed up to the present to get any encouragement from them.
He was then appealing for an increase in salary for these men. To-day I am appealing to this same gentleman, now Minister of Trade and Commerce, to use his influence with the government so as not to have this ten per cent struck against the salaries of the lower paid officials. If in 1929 they could not live on a salary of $1,040 or $1,080 a year how can they live to-day with a reduction of ten per cent, which leaves them $972, according to government figures-an amount requisite for them to obtain the bare necessaries of life.
I believe in the principle that in times of stress such as the country is now passing through every man, according to his means, should bear his share of the burden; but let us not take from the pockets of poor families this ten per cent which they need so badly if they are to carry on. Let the reduction be graded. Let it weigh upon the shoulders of those best able to bear it. If the government will ask for a graded reduction I will support it on any amount above $1,200; but I do oppose, with all my soul and all my strength, a reduction of ten per cent to the man who is earning only $1,200 a year. Ten per cent of a reduction leaves him only $972, while the bare necessaries of life will cost $965.

I am in a peculiar
position representing, as I do, an almost purely agricultural constituency. The people in my constituency have had to take a cut, not of ten per cent but of sixty or seventy per cent. Those who can scarcely get together the necessities of life are resentful of those who have enough and to spare.	.

When I returned $6,000 to the treasury I thought, and I still think that there is some moral value in suffering with those who have to suffer. This reducing of salaries and the slashing of commodity prices is economically unsound. We should have a different policy, one which would permit the issuing of more currency to be put into circulation without an accompanying burden of debt in the form of interest. I think that that should be done at once. I was interested in an article which appeared in last evening's Ottawa Journal, a reprint of an editorial of the Vancouver Sun. Mr. Speaker, I have no intention,
being a farmer, to take a very active part in this debate, seeing that others better 
qualified have thoroughly gone into the matter. May I, however, humbly express in the house, my views on the question submitted to us. At the outset, I must state that the terms of this resolution hold no surprise for me, and the more I acquire parliamentary experience and the more I take part in the work of the seventeenth parliament, the more I become convinced that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was not in earnest in 1930. I shall repeat for the hundredth time, as my colleagues and the Canadian people have done, that the electorate was shamefully deceived at the last election. It is true that those who sit on your right, sir, are not fond of having the surgeon's knife pry into the opened wound of their extravagant pledges in 1930; they shun the sight of the quivering wound-flesh caused by their foolish political eccentricities; however, it is our duty to scrutinize in this house all their pledges, so as to show them up to the people under their true light, in such a way that they will not in the future deceive the electorate as they did in 1930. The right hon. Prime Minister then travelled over the whole country, and everywhere he pledged himself to remedy all the evils borne by the people. He promised everywhere a wonderful prosperity, everywhere it was the same singsong: he was to revive in Canada bountiful days and turn the country into a marvellous land of Eden. But, with bankruptcy staring his administration in the face and his powerlessness to relieve all the ills from which the country suffered, he now appeals, in 1932, to the people to bear up in order to help him to administer the affairs of the country and thus permit him to remain in power. He furthermore appeals to the small wage-earners, the humble, the working classes, that they bleed themselves to death in order to balance a budget which hobbled along after the first eight months under his administration, limped very sadly this year, and probably will be crawling next year. After having pledged himself to relieve the people's distress, he exacts a ransom for bread and hunger from those to whom so much sympathy was shown in 1930.
In 1930, the Liberal party was blamed for the economic crisis, my leader was charged with all the evils from which the country suffered, he was made the scape-goat burdened with all the responsibilities for the distress [DOT]then existing. In 1932, the Government faced with the failure of its administration, and its helplessness to relieve the economic depression, endeavours to make amends, and instead of circumscribing the crisis, or viewing it as a

national problem, it now describes it as of
international character, as, after all, was the case in 1930. To-day faced with the impossibility of relieving the depression, the government states openly that this economic crisis in no way can be attributed to one country alone, but depends on uncontrollable circumstances, is of an international and worldwide character. Why did not the members sitting on the government benches acknowledge, in 1930, what they recognize to-day? Why did they not then view the crisis under its true aspect?
What did the Government do, after being placed in power, to relieve a'll the ills of which the liberal party was responsible, according to the conservative party? It called a special session, had $20,000,000 voted to relieve unemployment-an anti-social law in my opinion-it bungled up the tariff in all possible manner, once more neglecting agriculture for which so much sympathy was shown during the election. And to what purpose? To be followed by a general and much felt depression, an unemployment which spread in direct ratio of the square of the Government's incompetence. It ended in jeopardizing business and agriculture, and if there are here civil servants who hear me, allow me, sir, to tell them that if they are sacrificed by this government, agriculture had also its large share in these sacrifices. Last year, in the speech from the throne, four words were inserted on behalf of the farming class for which so much sympathy was shown; this year nothing was inserted, no allusion to agriculture is even made. I should like on this occasion to discuss agriculture at length, however, I shall have an * opportunity to refer to it later on in the session.
Prosperity was to flourish again and unemployment was to vanish. What result was attained? There is more poverty than ever, the unemployed are more numerous and notwithstanding the hard times, hundreds of civil servants are thrown on the street.
After having long sought to relieve the present depression, the Prime Minister, who on the day before had been torturing his brains to find a solution to the deplorable financial situation of the country by morning suddenly awakes, a flash of lightning seems to have illumined his thoughts and with a loud cry of "Eureka," he calls for the civil service list, slashes right and left, and on behalf of patriotism he calls upon all civil servants to sacrifice 10 per cent of their salary to help him in redeeming his election pledges. I quite agree that all should accept their share of sacrifices in the country's interest, and personally, I think that each should contribute
his quota to relieve the economic situation, but what I object to are the means adopted. This cut in salaries should be carried out not on the basis advocated, but on a graduated scale. As to the average and lower grades of civil servants, I agree with the Rev. Mr. Boileau, chaplain of the "Syndicats Catho-liques" of Montreal, that the measure proposed by this resolution is anti-social.
It is the custom in this House, to bring in support of the statements made, one's own preferred authorities. To support my own statement, I shall not have recourse to a letter written by a woman, whose name it is deemed proper not to divulge, a letter written by a woman ready to sacrifice herself for the country when it chances to please the right hon. Prime Minister, but I shall quote from an untouchable, undeniable, and indefectible authority, the authority of Rome.
In his henceforth unforgettable encyclical letter "Quadragesima Anno" the Roman Pontiff took up social questions and the following is what he states, speaking of the requirements of public welfare:
It is in the public interest that the workmen and employees should, after meeting the indispensable expenses, set aside part of their salary so as to build up a modest fortune.
And further he adds:
The estate must be sufficiently large to meet the needs of an honest living and to give the people some degree of comfort and culture which, providing a wise use is made of it, places no impediment to virtue, but on the contrary singularly facilitates its practice.
Instead of having recourse to this system of taxation, I think the government should have raised the rate of the income tax and taxed government bonds. The Dominion loan bonds last year was taken up in a very short period. Within a week we were informed that already $650,000,000 had been subscribed. Have you ever wondered why these millions were subscribed so quickly? I believe that a number of capitalists were anxious to shelter their capital by investing in state bonds. Probably there are amounts of $25,000, $50,000 or $100,000 in this subscription which do not pay a cent tax to the government, because they are not registered. Why were the wealthy people living in luxury, that is those who can most afford to pay, allowed to escape taxation? Thus the opinion of the authority which I have just quoted would have been followed, for speaking of activities of the state in social welfare, the following is what the encyclical letter says:
It behooves governments to protect the community and the individuals who form part of it, however in dealing with personal rights they must specially look after the weak and the poor.

If they contribute to the treasury $1,600, they still have a salary of $14,400. It is $400 more than the .ministers had under the King regime. While nobody suspected the plot, they so managed their own affairs that their salary was not affected, yet they are bold enough to place a tax of ten per cent on the small wage earners who are in receipt of $1,200, and on those whose income is $1,500, $1,800 or $2,000 per year. The employees who even now find it hard to get along with such salaries will be forced to contribute to the treasury $130, S140, $150 or $180 per year.
What effect will this measure have on the budget of those whose salaries put them in the average grade? A salary cut, that goes without saying, a decrease in purchasing power and therefore an upsetting of the family budget. Has anybody ever figured out what was the average cost of keeping a family of five persons? After consulting the Labour Gazette of February, 1932, at page 223, I find the following details, being the result of an inquiry held in sixty-nine towns of Canada: the following is the average cost per week for the upkeep of a family of five persons: food, including meat, butter, eggs, flour, peas, beans, sugar, vinegar, etc., $7.68 per week. No one will say that this is exaggerated. Heating and lighting $3.11 per week, rent $6.77 per week. Total expenditure per week $17.56. If you multiply this amount by 52 weeks you arrive at a total of $913.12 for the upkeep of a family of five persons per year.
Still according to the Labour Gazette one must further allow for clothes, underwear, and medical care or other unforeseen expenses, 50 per cent more, representing $456.53, which, added to the $913.12 brings up the total to $1,369.65. This is for the average class of civil servants. There still remains the lower grade to deal with. Let [DOT] us suppose, for a moment, that the latter only spend 30 per cent of the family expenditure for clothes, underwear, medical care or unforeseen expenses, we arrive at a total of $1,187.05.
How can you expect that a civil servant belonging to the average grade and having to

What is there that remains to these wage earners, to these employees to provide for the education and teaching of their children? Nothing. And yet,
The estate must be sufficiently large to meet the needs of an honest living and to give the people some degree of comfort and culture which, providing a wise use is made of it, places no impediment to virtue, but on the contrary singularly facilitates its practice.
Instead of taxing the small wage earner and the civil servant belonging to the average class, the government should increase somewhat the income tax, tax luxury but not the necessities, and ask those who can afford it, to contribute and not those who have already heavy expenses to meet.
It behooves governments to protect the community and the individuals who form part of it. however in dealing with personal rights they must specially look after the weak and the poor. The poor classes, on the contrary, without wealth to give them protection depend especially on the state for such protection. Let the state therefore be full of regard and solicitude for the workmen who belong to the poor classes.
Why does the Prime Minister seek with such stubbornness to introduce this arbitrary scale? He must have received protests from all parts of the country. To refreshen his memory, I shall quote a resolution adopted by the civil servants of Montreal, at a meeting held on February 22, 1932:
Whereas civil servants as a whole and particularly those whose salary is $2,000 or less did not draw remuneration proportionate to the increased cost of living when prosperity existed and everywhere salaries were raised.
Whereas the ten per cent will mean a greater loss, if the contribution made to the retiring fund (entirely paid by the employees) and the statutory increase which are to be cancelled, are taken into account.
Whereas this reduction will specially affect retail trade by decreasing the purchasing power.
Whereas civil servants have always been poorly remunerated.
Whereas the salary cut will affect the pensions.
Be it resolved that we request respectfully the government to modify its resolution relating to the cut of salaries by ten per cent, because it would not be fair that those who in no way benefited in prosperous times should be affected in such a radical way.

Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is endowed with exceptional qualities, I acknowledge it; but he has the defects of his qualities and those of certain small men. He realizes his perfections better than his failings. I would beg of him to act with care, and on the same score that he has requested this sacrifice from the civil servants, on behalf of patriotism, I also request him on behalf of the most integral patriotism not to disturb the small salaried men or those belonging to the average class; I further make this request on behalf of Christian justice, on behalf of Christian charity, on behalf of sound social doctrine.
As my good friend, the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) requested, I beg of him to introduce a bill in which humanism will predominate; and like the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I would advise him to be silent for a day, so as to prepare, in quietness and meditation, a more just and sound measure.

It is' my intention to take up the time of the house for only a very few minutes. I had not intended to participate in this debate; but after listening to the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite which covered the whole range of argument from the calm and rather dispassionate address of the former Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) to the speech which was delivered with such evangelistic fervour by the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), I believe there is one aspect of the case which no speaker except the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) discussed at all.
In the discussion of a reduction of wages, there are always two sides to be considered -the opinion of the employer and the opinion of the employees. We have heard at great length just how the employees may feel about this reduction; that it may in some cases work a slight hardship; but it was the hon. member for Southeast Grey only who gave us the considered opinion of the employer. In this case who is the employer of the civil servants of Canada? Is it the government? Is it parliament? No; it is the ten million people of Canada who pay the taxes, who are the employers. The hon. member for Southeast Grey has told us that the people of her constituency are very much in favour of this reduction; that they consider it reasonable. I have gone to the trouble to ascertain the opinions of some of the representative citizens of my constituency, both in the rural part and in the industrial section, and I believe it is the consensus of opinion that owing to the present depression throughout the world and the existing condition of affairs in Canada when it is absolutely necessary that reduction in expenditure shall be made, this reasonable reduction of ten per cent in the salaries of the civil servants of this country, is something that should be put into effect without delay. There have been advanced during the course of the debate by speakers from the opposition side many, shall I say rather queer arguments. The hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh), who time and again has proclaimed himself in the house and in the country as the great champion of Liberal principles, who has told us time and again what the great Liberal party-and it has been a great party-has stood for, in the course of his speech argued in favour of a capital levy. After listening to that address I came to the conclusion that the hon. member for North Battleford should transfer his seat to the far corner of that side of the house.
I was rather surprised that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) should put forth the idea, I believe in all seriousness, that the various government bouses throughout

Public Service-Salary Deduction	.
Canada should be closed at the present time and that all these great social functions which are held in different portions of the country- and I suppose the social functions in Ottawa would be included-should be dispensed with during the period of depression. To people who are out of work and others who are in receipt of low salaries this appeal, that these social functions engaged in by the wealthy, leisured class, should foe dispensed with, sounds very well. But do you know that some of these gentlemen who in appealing to the people of the country are democrats to the hilt, can 'be on other occasions aristocrats of the aristocrats? It was my good fortune recently to be in my room in the house when I saw passing down the corridor the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) dressed in his Windsor uniform, and a fine figure he made; he might have been taken right out of the pages of some romantic novel of .the middle ages. I am sure he may be proud that he has reached the place where he can wear that uniform. I do not in the least blame him for it, and I 'believe that the making of that uniform, the preparation of the material Oif which it consists, .the employment of the men who made it, and the men who from time to time press it or repair it or keep it in good condition,-all this provides wages and helps to give a certain number of people a living, or to .contribute to that end. And so, when these social functions are hold in various parts of the country, including the capital city, I suppose in the great majority of instances where beautiful gowns are worn .the ladies who wear them can afford to do so, and we Should remember that the making of the gowns has given work to hundreds of women who needed it. The retailing of the gowns 'has given reasonable profits to many merchants, and I for one am not in favour of having any of the social functions done away with, because it is one of the means by which people with money may be induced to part with it, thus providing work for those who would otherwise be unemployed at 'the present time.

But I have taken the trouble to ascertain from one of the leading merchants of my own county, a man who has been in business for a quarter of a century and who keeps a very accurate record of costs in every department of bis business, what the average reduction in the cost of living has been from the year 1930 up to the present time. The figures he has given after a very careful computation are these: Foodstuffs 27 to 29 per cent; dry goods 22 to 25 per cent; and boots and shoes from 18 to 20 per cent. And these reductions apply all along the line in all classes of commodities. I am sure therefore that any civil servant whose salary has been reduced by ten per cent will find it easier to make both ends meet during the coming year than he could formerly with his salary as it was but with prices higher.
The hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) made somewhat contemptuous allusion to the mounted police, the forces of law and order. As a citizen of Canada. I am proud of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and I think every other citizen of this dominion should be equally proud of them. There is no body of men holding similar positions and doing similar work in any country in the world more worthy of the support and admiration of all citizens of the country employing them than is this fine body of men. 1 am sure we should be glad that men who possess so much tact and common sense and so great an ability to get along with people in a reasonable way, men who are able to quell disturbances with a minimum of trouble, are in our midst, and on every occasion we should do all that we can to support and strengthen that organization.
The civil servants of Canada are just as reasonable as any other citizens of this country. I have had occasion to discuss this question with various members of that fine body and I believe that we have a civil service in Canada the equal of any other service of the kind in the world. In my own county there are a large number of civil servants employed in two or three departments. They are very efficient men and I believe that, as reasonable people, they will regard this reduction as fair. It has been announced that it is for only one year, and we know that if times improve and conditions are better, the civil servants will have their former salaries restored in course of time.

class? The income tax exempts a married man up to $3,000. That being so, what is the justification of a demand that a civil servant getting $1,200 should contribute $60?

12,000	and 15,000. If I am correctly informed, since last fall the civil servants have been paying so much a week from their salaries into a fund to help the unemployed, and they pay five per cent for superannuation also. Now they are to be reduced ten per cent, and they will not get their annual increases, so certainly they are suffering more than the farmers, who at least can grow many of the necessities of life. The income tax takes into account family charges; a married man with a family receives a much greater exemption than a single man or a married man without a family. This principle was applied to the income tax during the war, and it should be applied now in connection with this reduction.
The Conservatives in my riding stated the other night that certainly this reduction would set a bad example to provincial and municipal governments, private industries and merchants, who might follow the lead of this government and reduce the salaries of their employees, which are none too high at the present time. When the example is set by the federal government certainly it has more weight than it would have coming from a private corporation. Speaking in Ottawa in July, 1930, the Prime Minister expressed the view that he could render the civil service more efficient by keeping those wtho fulfilled the duties of their position most capably, paying 'them adequate salaries, and dismissing the others. But since that time no steps have been taken to attain that objective; the fust thing to be done by this government is to make this reduction and to dismiss quite a number of civil servants.
When this resolution was presented to the house we heard on the streets the complaints of civil servants, but for the last few days members of the service have become shy and bashful, and they do mot discus the matter. They are afraid of losing their jobs. Right after the introduction of this resolution the Department of Public Works served notice on eighty-two temporary employees that their

services would mot be required beyond the end of this month. Now members of the public service are afraid to look around, in the fear that to-morrow morning they may find themselves in the ranks of the unemployed.
If this reduction were graded, starting at say $2,000, certainly there would not be such protests as we have heard. I find that the bon. member f-or New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was told that only 805 employees of the public service were receiving salaries of more than $4,000 and that their contribution under this measure would be about $400,000. This means that some $7,900,000 will have to be contributed by civil servants receiving less than $4,000 a year. It has been stated that the average salary in the civil service is about $1,500 a year, so it will be seen that the lower paid civil servants will have to contribute the greater portion of the $8,300,000 which the Prime Minister said would be saved by this reduction. In 1929 it was stated in this house that there were 3,779 male civil servants in Ottawa receiving less than $100 a month, and at that time the average salary of civil servants in this city was $1,650.
This measure was brought in by the Prime Minister in order to balance the budget; he wants $8,300,000 from the civil service for that purpose. I do not know what will be the deficit, but certainly -this amount will not cover it this year, and certainly the civil servants will suffer more than those employed in private industry. I desire to voice as forcibly as I can the views of the people in my riding and of the others who have written to me with reference to this subject matter. I trust the Prime Minister will reconsider his decision as to this ten per cent cut and draft a bill which will graduate the reduction to be made in the civil service salaries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the civil service of a country, is the mechanism through which the government enforces its laws and collects the necessary returns for the good administration of the country. The civil service of Canada is the best medium under these circumstances to give the country a good government after the legislation we enact receives the sanction of the Governor General and the necessary regulations are passed by orders in council.
Our civil service, sir, is an excellent one. I rise this evening to champion its cause. We are aware that our civil service, copied on the English system, is not far from being perfect. The hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Shaver) stated that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was a first class body of men. I state that the civil service also belongs to that class. I have the same admiration for the Royal Mounted Police as the hon. member has. On the other hand, if in India England can control 327,000,000 people with a civil service list of 11,000 employees and 55,000 soldiers, it only proves that we have in Canada a perfect system whose endeavours deserve to be recognized.
The service is open to those who are. gifted. One must undergo a test. I have often seen, after the examinations, the questions submitted to candidates. It is as difficult, to-day, to pass the civil service examinations as it is to obtain a certificate in our business colleges. I shall even state that in certain fields of activity, for instance in the Trade and Commerce department, it is as difficult to pass the test as it is to obtain a bachelor's degree in our classical colleges. Many of our young people after finishing their studies in colleges enter the civil service and believe that they

are filling lucrative positions, they believe that prospects are bright for their talents and that they will become experts. They pass the required tests and are given a fixed salary; they carry on with this salary and its statutory increases; they regulate their budget accordingly and work conscientiously, from the humble servant in the Public Works up to the officials of the Post Office Department, Marine, Customs and External Affairs.
We are asked, to-day, by this resolution to cut down their remuneration, their salary by ten per cent. It is the duty of the government to remunerate their employees. If we want the country to conform with the legislation we enact we must set the example. If the government does not sufficiently remunerate its servants or does not conform with the statutes which provide for salaries and statutory increases, I state that this is a very poor example to give to the industrial commercial and farming classes of this country.
These civil servants, as I stated a moment ago, have so regulated their budget, knowing that their limit had been reached, nevertheless endeavouring not only to provide for the necessary things but to afford some small luxuries during their lifetime. To-day, they are told:	we cut you down 10 per cent from
81,200 up. An employee who earns $1,225, will have to pay 8122.50 plus five per cent to the pensions fund; he would be better off if his salary was reduced by $25, so that he could be classed in the $1,200. He would then have only $60 as the government would also pay $60, to contribute to pensions fund.
Has this phase of the question been examined? I have not thoroughly studied the Civil Service Pensions Act, it however strikes me that thanks to this yearly five per cent, since its inception, millions must have accumulated in the treasury. Why does not the government come to an understanding with the Civil Service Federation of Canada? Why does it not borrow from the Pension fund? Why not borrow from that source the five or six million dollars needed to cover this year's exigencies, seeing that the Prime Minister stated the other day to the delega-gation that it would only be for a year?
Banks are being merged, anything can be done to-day through legislation or orders in council, except change a man into a woman! Why not borrow from the civil service pensions fund an amount equal to this salary cut, adopt the necessary resolutions, have regular meetings, bridge over the deficit and the spreads appearing in the year's budget. Desperate ills require desperate remedies! If, this year, it is found necessary to reduce the civil servants' salaries, why not take the

equivalent from their pensions fund. It is better to borrow it to-day and not have them default their financial obligations, rather than pay them a pension in twenty or twenty-five years hence when perhaps they will not need it. This is the time to satisfy those who, by statute, have a right to their salary so that they may live as in the past and provide for their children's education. We must act in such a way that the tradespeople be not despoiled of their fair profit and the business community be not deprived of this ten per cent which civil servants spend either in clothes, food or even, let us be frank, as it is their right, for themselves and family, in pleasure resorts.
I read lately in an Ottawa newspaper that the amount deducted from the civil servants' salaries will deprive the tradespeople of $2,000,000. Two million dollars taken from the local trade, is an enormous amount. Merchants as well as manufacturers will have to bear the loss. If the purchasing power is lacking, less sales will take place and the people of Ottawa as well as of Canada will suffer from it, its effect will be felt in all fields of industrial and commercial activities.
I also read lately in an American newspaper -it is well to make contrasts for we are quite close to the United States border-that President Hoover gave out the following statement, he who has under his jurisdiction
600,000	United States civil servants:
I have no intention to cut down the salaries; we must not reduce them; the purchasing power must not be lacking; we must not upset this service which is devoted to its work and needs the whole of its salary in order to give a good service to the state, help us to make of the United States a greater country and assist us in making the American republic a country of future still greater. However, owing to our heavy debts, if it is absolutely necessary, we shall reduce the number of employees but we shall maintain their salary on the level where it is to-day.
What is happening in Canada? By this resolution it is intended to cut the salaries, and pursuant to notices sent out the number of employees have already been reduced. On the one hand, the purchasing power of the permanent civil servants is decreased, while on the other hand, the temporary employees are dismissed, they that have, for the last few years, given the best of their life and energy in the hope of being taken in the service. In Montreal alone 120 are thrown on the street.
Under such circumstances, is this fair? I say no. The government must readjust its budget by applying, if necessary, to the magnates of finance. I am neither a communist nor a bolshevist, however, let those

who have an income of $500,000 or $600,000, if necessary, contribute $400,000 to the state for a year, they still will have plenty to live upon with $200,000. Let heirs of estates who have never done a stroke of work to build up such fortunes and have thousands of dollars to spend yearly, let them, I say, contribute three-quarters of their wealth to the state for a year, let them follow the example of the right hon. Mr. Baldwin, President of the Council in England, whom I admire, and who generously gave to the treasury $625,000, representing the profits he made during the war, he handed over this amount to his country, saying that it was the price of blood. His son lately stated in an interview:
My father's income is less than it was in 1909, however he can live on it; our family still lives in great comfort.
Let those who can afford to do so make contributions to the treasury! Let them help the government to put order in their finances, let them contribute in putting the administration on its feet; I trust they will be induced to do so, because if our country is prosperous, so will we all be. All classes of the community will benefit by it and an alleluia of joy will be heard throughout the country. But allow the civil servants to live in peace in the discharge of their duties. I am aware that this resolution will carry. I have no illusions. During the ten years of my parliamentary life, I have learned that majorities rule in this house and all measures are enacted through these majorities, otherwise they would amount to motions of nonconfidence adopted by the ruling party. We, that belong to the opposition have very little influence in this house, however, we are on the watch like vestals, endeavouring to keep the fire of the Liberal party burning so that our friends all over Canada may see the flame through the window panes of this house; "Keep the fires burning." We do our best to keep our lighthouse continuously lit. There is not much oil left in the tank but the wick is good and the light is still bright. What I would suggest, under the circumstances, since I am convinced that this measure will carry: That the government make no cut in salaries under $4,000. From $4,000 deduct four per cent, if it so desires; $5,000 deduct five per cent'; $6,000, six per cent; $7,000, seven per cent; $8,000, eight per cent; $9,000, nine per cent, and $10,000, ten per cent. That would be a fair and reasonable measure, and I think that civil servants would be satisfied and continue to live with the hope of meeting their obligations. I am not saying this in
order to complain about the $400 which I shall, as a member, have to pay the 6tate. No, sir, I shall graciously do so; I shall do my bit generously, under the circumstances, and contribute to the treasury. It will make me happier to think that I have contributed, in the opposition, to help the government in the administration of the country, by my humble subscription of $400.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with
rapt attention to the words of wisdom of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson). It must be clearly understood that those who live in the cities of this dominion are not responsible for the industrial system under which they live. That system was brought into being by men whose chief motive was profit, and in a period of depression such as that through which we are passing, it is only natural in the sequence of events that those unfortuate individuals should suffer until such time as the government of this country assume the responsibility which is theirs towards the men and women who find themselves in their present situation under circumstances over which they have no control.
I know of nothing easier than to get up in a deliberate assembly such as this and suggest that the men and women who spend their lives working in the factories of this dominion should go into the vacant wastes of northern Ontario and, without any previous experience, without any capital and, in many instances, suffering from malnutrition, carve out a livelihood there for themselves. For many years organized labour, through the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, has made suggestions to the federal government along the same lines as those made by the hon. member for Lanark this evening. I trust that he will use his influence with the government of the day to see that such a policy is put into effect and carried out, so that those men who are fitted for a life on the farm can leave our cities, thus lessening the acute situation brought about by unemployment, and at least earn their sustenance on the lands of this country. I readily understand the position in which the farmers of the country find themselves. The first urge of life is to secure food, clothing and shelter, yet many thousands of the industrial workers in our cities are not in a position to obtain the necessaries of life in such measure as to ensure for themselves, and consequently for future Canadians, full bodily health and strength. I say this from my experience as a member of the hospital board in the city

Public Service-Salary Deduction
from which I come and a member for some years of the board of health of that city, where thousands of undernourished children pass through these two organizations.

I will come to that in
a moment. Many of these civil servants are living in modern industrial and commercial cities; they are trying to get along on a thousand dollars or less per annum, endeavouring to bring up families. The hon. member who has asked that question will readily understand what bearing my remarks have on the question before us. The civil servants were not responsible for the condition that exists to-day. Had the government not made the twenty per cent discount in income taxation last year they would have been in a better position to-day, and this proposed reduction in salaries could have been largely avoided. From our experience, we of the labour movement know that every reduction in wages merely intensifies the present condition; it reflects itself in business, in industry and in agriculture, in the reduced consuming power of the people affected.
We have a paradox to-day in this, that the governments of this country are lowering the standard of living of their employees on the one hand, while on the other hand they are guaranteeing to the moneylenders increased returns on the money they borrow. The ramifications of this policy are felt far and wide. After all, what is the collateral of the money which is lent to the government of the country? It is the earning power of the men and women employed in industry and agriculture; and when the government in the midst of intense industrial depression offers to the moneylenders of the country rates of interest of five per cent and over in connection, for example, with the recent national service loan, the natural consequence is that when the provinces go to the country for money their interest rates are raised. The province of Ontario recently floated a loan bearing interest at the rate of over six per cent, and it was snapped up within three hours of the time it was issued. And why not? What better security can you have than the government of that province if you have the money to lend? But what chance have the municipalities to borrow money at lower rates than are offered by the provincial or the federal government? The cities throughout the dominion, those that can borrow money, are forced to pay more than the provinces or the federal government.

Then we come to the most important factor of all-the wage earners of the country who are trying to buy their own homes. These people are carrying mortgages at the present time at probably six per cent or a little better. What chance have they, in these circumstances, of renewing those mortgages at such figures? It is obvious that the security of the workingman's home or farm is not considered such a sound security as government bonds, and what is to become of these people? I predict that thousands of workingmen and women will lose their homes in the next twelve months or two years, and thousands of farmers their farms, and so the whole thing is being pyramided
At the last session of parliament an order in council was passed by the federal government dealing with unemployment relief, and there appeared in it the following provision:
Unless a modification of this requirement is previously agreed to by the minister, the provincial or municipal authorities may fix rates of wages to be paid, provided that such rates be fair and reasonable and not in excess of the rates required to be paid by the federal government for the character or class of work in the district.
Now, if it is logical for the parliament of Canada to fix a maximum rate of wages for human labour, is it not just as logical in the interests of the country, in a national emergency, to fix maximum rates of interest demanded by the bondholders of Canada? You cannot make the man on the street believe that if increased demands on lenders is not made this country of ours will be ruined. We have to remember that the reduction in wages hits a body of workers in this country who in many instances have no means of defending themselves. Cutting the salaries of civil servants is like throwing a stone in the water from which the ripples pass on to places beyond the human eye. Naturally these servants live right up to their incomes because, in the majority of cases, the incomes do not permit of any other course. In this debate we have heard the suggestion many times that the people should save. When one surveys the wages paid the civil servants in this dominion one might conclude that in the great majority of cases it would be economically impossible to save very much. The effect of the cut will be that food will be cut down, doctors will lose, and dentists will lose.

I do not intend to suggest what certain selfish manufacturing interests would do under present conditions, but I believe it is the duty of this government, and of every provincial and municipal government, to see that none of their employees works under salary scales below the minimum standard of civilized communities. I think my position is sound, and it is backed by the labour movement of Canada.
Another angle of the problem presents itself. While I freely admit .that the price of food has declined, yet the major items in the ordinary family budget of one who lives in a city are coal, rent, insurance and other uncontrollable expenditures. In those items there has been very little reduction. We will see, therefore, that if any reduction is to be made in the family budget it will -have to be made on account of the reduction in food prices. Some hon. members have spoken about the judges. I am not -a lawyer, but I do not know of any British institution which does not control its own destiny. If the government of the day so desired, undoubtedly judges' salaries -could be cut; there is no question about that.
Then, we consider the man who enjoys a large salary. In -contrast we find the lower salaried employee who has to cut down his living budget to feed his family. Opposed to that we have the man who receives $10,000 a year who may have to curtail a few luxuries, and may not be able to make so many investments or put so much money in the bank, but whose real standard of living, so far as the provision of food for himself and his family is concerned, irrespective of this cut, will remain unimpaired.
Being a trade unionist of many years standing, and having passed through the struggle for the adoption of the principle of collective bargaining, I know of no reason why the government of the day should not have taken the same action as any other corporation or organization wishing to make savings. The labour people of Canada look with amazement at the present attitude of the government. This cut was made in a spirit of take-it-or-leave-it; the decision was taken without any regard for living conditions or salaries earned by the employees concerned. We believe that the government at least should have reflected the spirit of its own Labour department and referred the matter to a -board of arbitration or conciliation, thereby permitting 'the various organizations of civil servants at least to endeavour to defend their own membership.
In conclusion, I think it is -the general opinion of all hon. members that no person during the course of this depression should suffer want, whether he be engaged in agriculture, business, the professions, or industry.
I know of no better way to ensure this condition than that the rate of income tax from those receiving, we will say, $150 a month and up, be on a -graduated scale to supply funds to help maintain those who, through no fault of their own, to-day find themselves unemployed.
